lessons: Check several candidates, even before options become scarce. Compare how many other offered stones retain poses and whether currently unplaceable stones regain them; protect stones with few poses. A zero is a warning, not proof of permanent loss, and a one-step check cannot guarantee completion.

Favor substantial LLC over a sharp early drop made to gain NHR, IWR or LFR. Do not maximize LLC blindly: a lower-LLC placement may be necessary to keep stones placeable, and the current score does not guarantee the finished wall’s load.

Favor good GDS and near-zero LFR while seeking reasonable interlocking; avoid sacrificing fit or stability for a single spectacular IWR. Compare GDS with the current alternatives: a raw zero can be tied for best, particularly at a new course.

Treat tall, narrow rotations cautiously early, especially when they give up LLC or density for interlocking. A near-zero NHR only levels the stone with its left neighbour; balance it against fit and interlocking rather than maximizing it at every placement.

messages.content:
You study finished dry-stone walls and write lessons for the builder of later walls.
The builder. A wall is built course by course with Wang's method. At each placement some of the remaining stones are on offer (all of them once only a few are left), and the builder chooses one candidate: a stone on offer in one of four rotations, at the position Wang's image convolution found for it. Every candidate is feasible. Of each candidate the builder sees the rotation, the width and height of its bounding box in pixels and Wang's five filter scores (higher is better for each): NHR course height (0 = level with its left neighbour), GDS global density, IWR interlocking (its vertical joint far from the joints below), LLC the kinematic limit load of the wall with the stone added and stabilized, divided by the friction coefficient, LFR local void (0 = flush on the left and on the bottom). The builder also sees n_remaining, the stones not yet placed; a summary of the current wall, where the skyline is the height of the wall's top above the ground at each column, in pixels (h_max its maximum, h_range maximum minus minimum, h_std its standard deviation, void_under_skyline_px the empty pixels below it, n_skyline_jumps its steps of more than 3 pixels between neighbouring columns); and the stones on offer that have no feasible candidate now. Before choosing, the builder may call check_after for some candidates: how many feasible poses every other stone on offer would have at the next placement if that candidate were placed (0: that stone could not be placed next). The builder knows nothing about the finished wall.
The goal. A finished wall is judged on four metrics: F_SF, stone filling (the share of the wall area that is stone, higher is better); F_AH, the horizontal joint path index (lower is better: no long continuous horizontal joints); F_AV, the vertical joint path index (higher is better: vertical joints are staggered); F_LR, the smaller of the left and right kinematic limit loads of the wall divided by the friction coefficient (higher is better). All four must be good, and a stone that cannot be placed is lost to the wall: losing stones is worse than a lower metric.
The data. stone_sets lists sets of stones. The walls of one set were built from the same stones in the same place and differ only in the choices made at the placements; never compare walls of different sets. They were built by fixed rules (the five scores applied in a fixed order of priority), without check_after. Of each set's n_walls_ranked walls you get 4: two labelled good (the highest mean_z among the walls that placed the most stones), one of lower quality (the lowest mean_z among those) and one that lost stones (the fewest placed). Per wall: placed and lost count stones; metrics gives each metric's value and z, its z-score among the set's walls with the sign turned so that higher is always better; mean_z is the mean of the four z; rank is the wall's place by mean_z among the set's walls (1 is the best); first_placement_differing_from_wall_1 is the first placement at which the wall and the set's first wall differ (null: none); stopped_with, on a wall that lost stones, is n_remaining and the wall summary when no remaining stone could be placed. placements has one row per stone placed, in the order of placement_columns: placement (from 1), n_remaining, n_candidates (the feasible candidates there), n_unplaceable (the stones on offer without one), the wall summary before the placement, then the rotation, width and height of the candidate that was placed and its five scores, each followed by its share: the share of that placement's candidates whose score is not higher (1.0: no candidate scored higher; a low share: the choice gave that score up).
Your task. Within each set compare the good walls with the bad ones, look for what recurs across sets, and write at most 5 lessons for the builder. A lesson is one line of at most 60 words that the builder can apply at a placement from what it sees there: the candidates' scores and bounding boxes, the wall summary, n_remaining, the unplaceable stones, check_after. Do not mention particular stones, sets, walls or coordinates. Prefer what several sets support to what one wall suggests; write fewer than 5 lessons if the data support fewer. Finish with commit_lessons, with an empty text for each lesson you do not write.
